chapters.title: Narrative Continued by the Doctor: How the Ship Was Abandoned
paragraphs: It was about half past one — three bells, in sea talk — when the two boats put off from the HISPANIOLA and went ashore. The captain, the squire, and I were talking things over in the cabin. Had there been a breath of wind, we'd have fallen on the six mutineers left aboard with us, slipped our cable, and stood out to sea. But there was no wind; and, to crown our helplessness, down came Hunter with word that Jim Hawkins had slipped into a boat and gone ashore with the rest.

It never crossed our minds to doubt Jim Hawkins, but we feared for his safety. With the men in the temper they were in, it seemed an even chance whether we'd see the lad again. We hurried on deck. The pitch was bubbling in the seams; the foul stench of the place turned my stomach; if ever a man smelt fever and dysentery, it was in that vile anchorage. The six rogues sat grumbling under a sail in the forecastle; ashore we could see the gigs made fast, with a man sitting in each, close by where the river runs in. One of them was whistling “Lillibullero.”
Waiting told on the nerves, and it was settled that Hunter and I should go ashore in the jolly-boat to find out what we could.

The gigs had borne off to their right, but Hunter and I pulled straight in, toward the stockade marked on the chart. The two men left guarding the boats seemed thrown into a flurry at the sight of us; “Lillibullero” broke off, and I could see the pair arguing what they ought to do. Had they gone and told Silver, things might have fallen out quite otherwise; but they had their orders, I suppose, and chose to sit tight where they were and fall back on “Lillibullero.”

There was a slight bend in the coast, and I steered to put it between us, so that even before we landed the gigs were out of our sight. I jumped out and came as near a run as I dared, a big silk handkerchief under my hat against the heat, and a brace of pistols primed and ready for safety.
Not a hundred yards on, I had reached the stockade.

This is how it lay: a spring of clear water rose almost at the top of a knoll. On the knoll, and enclosing the spring, they had built a stout loghouse, big enough at a pinch to hold two-score people, and loopholed for musket-fire on every side. All round it they had cleared a wide open space, and the whole was finished off with a six-foot paling, with neither door nor gap — too strong to pull down without time and labour, too open to give the attackers any cover. The people inside had every advantage: they could stand quiet under shelter and pick the others off like partridges. All they needed was a careful watch and food enough; short of being utterly surprised, they could have held the place against a regiment.

What took my fancy above all was the spring. For though we were well enough placed in the cabin of the HISPANIOLA — plenty of arms and ammunition, food, excellent wines — one thing had been overlooked: we had no water. I was turning this over when there rang out across the island the cry of a man at the point of death. I am no stranger to violent death — I served his Royal Highness the Duke of Cumberland, and took a wound myself at Fontenoy — but I know my pulse went all to pieces. “Jim Hawkins is done for,” was my first thought.

It is something to have been a soldier, but more still to have been a doctor. In our trade there's no time for dithering. So I made up my mind on the instant, and with no time lost went back to the shore and jumped into the jolly-boat.
Hunter, by good fortune, was a strong oar; we fairly made the water fly, and in no time the boat was alongside and I back aboard the schooner.
I found them all shaken, as was only natural. The squire was sitting down, white as a sheet, brooding on the harm he'd led us into — good soul; and one of the six forecastle hands was little better.

“There's a man,” says Captain Smollett, with a nod toward him, “new to this kind of work. He came near fainting, doctor, when he heard that cry. Another touch on the tiller and that fellow would come over to us.”
I laid my plan before the captain, and between us we worked out the particulars of carrying it through.

Old Redruth we stationed in the gallery between cabin and forecastle, with three or four loaded muskets and a mattress to shield him. Hunter worked the boat round under the stern-port, and Joyce and I fell to loading her — tins of powder, muskets, biscuit-bags, kegs of pork, a cask of brandy, and my precious medicine chest.
Meanwhile the squire and the captain stayed on deck, and the captain hailed the coxswain, the chief man left aboard.
“Mr. Hands,” said he, “here are two of us, with a brace of pistols each. If any one of you six makes a signal of any kind, that man's a dead man.”

They were taken aback, and after a little muttering together, the whole lot tumbled down the fore companion — meaning, no doubt, to take us in the rear. But when they found Redruth waiting for them in the railed gallery, they went about at once, and a single head popped up again on deck.
“Down, dog!” cries the captain.
And the head ducked back; and for the time we heard no more of these six very faint-hearted seamen.

By now, pitching things in as fast as they came, we had the jolly-boat loaded as deep as we dared. Joyce and I got out through the stern-port and pulled for shore again as hard as the oars would drive us.

This second trip fairly roused the watchers along the shore. “Lillibullero” stopped once more; and just before we lost sight of them behind the little point, one of them whipped ashore and was gone. I half thought of changing my plan and smashing their boats, but I feared Silver and the others might be close at hand, and that we might lose everything by reaching for too much.

We soon touched land in the same spot as before and set to stocking the blockhouse. All three of us made the first trip, heavily loaded, and pitched our stores over the palisade. Then, leaving Joyce to guard them — one man, true, but with half a dozen muskets — Hunter and I went back to the jolly-boat and loaded ourselves once more. So we kept on, never stopping for breath, until the whole cargo was stowed; whereupon the two servants took post in the blockhouse, and I, with all my strength, sculled back to the HISPANIOLA.

That we ventured a second boatload sounds bolder than it really was. They had the numbers, of course, but we had the arms. Not a man ashore carried a musket, and before they could come within pistol-range we flattered ourselves we could give a good account of half a dozen at least.

At the stern window the squire stood waiting, his faintness clean gone. He caught the painter, made it fast, and the two of us loaded the boat for dear life. The cargo was pork, powder, and biscuit, with no more than a musket and a cutlass each for the squire, myself, Redruth, and the captain. The rest of the arms and powder went over the side into two and a half fathoms, where we could see the bright steel glinting far down in the sun on the clean sand.

By now the tide had begun to ebb, and the ship was swinging round to her anchor. Voices could be heard faintly hallooing over toward the two gigs; and though that eased our minds for Joyce and Hunter, well to the eastward, it warned our own party to be gone.
Redruth quit his post in the gallery and let himself down into the boat, and we worked her round to the ship's counter, the handier for Captain Smollett.
“Now, men,” said he, “do you hear me?”
No answer came from the forecastle.
“It's to you, Abraham Gray — it's you I'm speaking to.”
Still no reply.

“Gray,” the captain went on, a little louder, “I'm leaving this ship, and I order you to follow your captain. I know you're a good man at bottom, and I dare say not one of the lot of you is as bad as he makes out. Here's my watch in my hand; I give you thirty seconds to come over to me.”
There was a pause.
“Come, my fine fellow,” the captain went on; “don't hang in stays so long. I'm risking my own life and these good gentlemen's every second of it.”
Then came a sudden scuffle, the sound of blows, and out burst Abraham Gray with a knife-cut down one cheek, and came running to the captain like a dog to the whistle.
“I'm with you, sir,” said he.
And in the next moment he and the captain were aboard with us, and we had pushed off and pulled away.
Out of the ship we were — but not yet safe ashore in the stockade.

chapters.title: Narrative Continued by the Doctor: The Jolly-boat’s Last Trip
paragraphs: This fifth trip was quite unlike any of the others. For one thing, the little cockleshell of a boat we were in was badly overloaded. Five grown men — three of them, Trelawney, Redruth, and the captain, over six feet tall — were already more than she was built to carry. Add to that the powder, the pork, the bread-bags. The gunwale was lipping water astern. Several times we shipped a little, and my breeches and coat-tails were soaked through before we'd gone a hundred yards.
The captain made us trim the boat, and we got her riding a little more evenly. Even so, we hardly dared breathe.

For another thing, the ebb was now setting — a strong rippling current running westward through the basin, then turning south and seaward down the straits we'd come in by that morning. The very ripples were a danger to our overloaded craft; but the worst of it was that the current swept us off our true course, away from the proper landing-place behind the point. Let it have its way, and we'd come ashore right beside the gigs, where the pirates might show up at any moment.

“I can't hold her head for the stockade, sir,” I told the captain. The tiller was mine, while he and Redruth, the two fresh hands, took the oars. “The tide keeps washing her down. Could you pull a bit harder?”
“Not without swamping her,” said he. “You must bear up, sir, if you please — bear up till you see you're gaining.”
I tried, and found by trial that the tide kept sweeping us westward until I'd laid her head due east — pretty near at right angles to the way we wanted to go.
“We'll never make the shore at this rate,” said I.

“If that's the only course we can lie, sir, then lie it we must,” returned the captain. “We've to keep upstream. You see, sir,” he went on, “once we dropped to leeward of the landing-place, there's no saying where we'd fetch up, besides the chance of being boarded by the gigs; whereas, the way we're heading, the current's bound to slacken, and then we can work back along the shore.”
“The current's easing already, sir,” said the man Gray, who sat in the bows; “you can let her off a bit.”
“Thank you, my man,” said I, just as if nothing had happened — for we'd all quietly made up our minds to treat him as one of ourselves.
Then suddenly the captain spoke again, and his voice, I thought, was a little altered.
“The gun!” said he.
“I've thought of that,” said I, supposing he meant a bombardment of the fort. “They could never get the gun ashore; and if they did, they'd never haul it through the woods.”
“Look astern, doctor,” the captain answered.

We'd clean forgotten the long nine; and there, to our horror, were the five rogues hard at work about her, stripping off her “jacket,” as they called the stout tarpaulin she sailed under. And in the same instant it flashed on me that the round-shot and the powder for the gun had been left behind, and that one stroke of an axe would put the whole of it into the villains' hands.
“Israel was Flint's gunner,” said Gray, hoarsely.

At any risk, we put the boat's head straight for the landing-place. By now we were so far out of the current's run that we kept steerage-way even at our slow, careful stroke, and I could hold her steady for the goal. But the worst of it was that the course I now had to steer turned our broadside, instead of our stern, to the HISPANIOLA, and made of us a target like a barn door.
I could hear, as well as see, that brandy-faced rascal Israel Hands thumping a round-shot down on the deck.
“Who's the best shot?” asked the captain.
“Mr. Trelawney, far and away,” said I.
“Mr. Trelawney, would you pick me off one of those men, sir? Hands, if you can,” said the captain.
Cool as steel, Trelawney looked to his priming.
“Now,” cried the captain, “easy with that gun, sir, or you'll swamp us. All hands stand ready to trim her as he aims.”
The squire raised his gun, the rowing stopped, and we leaned over to the other side to hold the balance; and it was all so neatly managed that we never shipped a drop.

By now they'd slewed the gun round on its swivel, and Hands, at the muzzle with the rammer, was the most exposed of them. Still, our luck was out, for just as Trelawney fired, Hands stooped down, the ball whistled over him, and it was one of the other four who fell.

The cry he gave was taken up not only by his mates aboard but by a great many voices from the shore; and looking that way I saw the other pirates pouring out from among the trees and tumbling into their places in the boats.
“Here come the gigs, sir,” said I.
“Give way, then,” cried the captain. “Never mind if we swamp her now. If we can't make the shore, it's all up with us.”
“Only one gig's being manned, sir,” I added; “the other crew are most likely going round by the shore to head us off.”

“They'll have a hot run of it, sir,” returned the captain. “Jack ashore is no great shakes. It's not them I mind; it's the round-shot. Carpet bowls! The squire's lady's-maid couldn't miss. Tell us when you see the match, squire, and we'll hold water.”

Meanwhile we'd been making fair headway for so loaded a boat, and had shipped only a little water doing it. We were close in now — thirty or forty strokes and we'd beach her, for the ebb had already bared a narrow belt of sand below the clustering trees. The gig was no longer to be feared; the little point had hidden it from us. The ebb-tide, that had used us so cruelly, was now making amends and holding back our pursuers. The one danger left was the gun.
“If I dared,” said the captain, “I'd lie to and pick off another man.”
But it was plain they meant to let nothing hold up their shot. They never so much as glanced at their fallen mate, though he wasn't dead — I could see him trying to crawl away.
“Ready!” cried the squire.
“Hold!” cried the captain, quick as an echo.

And he and Redruth backed with a great heave that drove her stern clean under water. The report came at the same instant. This was the first that Jim heard — the squire's shot hadn't carried to him. Where the ball went, none of us rightly knew; but I fancy it must have passed over our heads, and that the wind of it may have helped on our mishap.

In any case the boat settled by the stern, gently enough, in three feet of water, leaving the captain and me on our feet, face to face. The other three went clean under and came up streaming and gasping.

So far there was no great harm. No lives lost, and we could wade ashore safely enough. But all our stores were on the bottom; and, worse, only two of our five guns were fit to use. Mine I'd snatched from my knees and held over my head, by a sort of instinct. The captain had carried his slung over his shoulder by a bandoleer, and, like a wise man, lock uppermost. The other three had gone down with the boat.

To add to our worries, we could already hear voices drawing near in the woods along the shore; and we had not only the danger of being cut off from the stockade in our half-crippled state, but the fear of whether Hunter and Joyce, if a half-dozen fell on them, would have the sense and steadiness to hold firm. Hunter we could count on; Joyce was a doubtful case — a pleasant, polite fellow for a valet, good at brushing a coat, but hardly cut out for a man of war.
With all this in mind, we waded ashore as fast as we could, leaving the poor jolly-boat behind us, and a good half of all our powder and provisions with her.

chapters.title: Narrative Continued by the Doctor: End of the First Day’s Fighting
paragraphs: We made what speed we could across the strip of wood that now lay between us and the stockade, and at every step the buccaneers' voices rang nearer. Soon we could hear their footfalls as they ran, and the cracking of the branches as they forced through a patch of thicket.
I began to see we'd have a real brush of it, and looked to my priming.
“Captain,” said I, “Trelawney's our dead shot. Give him your gun — his own's no good.”

They swapped guns, and Trelawney — silent and cool as he'd been since the trouble began — paused a moment on his heel to see all was fit for service. At the same time, noticing Gray had no weapon, I handed him my cutlass. It did all our hearts good to see him spit on his hand, knit his brows, and make the blade sing through the air. Every line of him showed that our new hand was worth his salt.

Forty paces more brought us to the edge of the wood, with the stockade before us. We struck the fence about the middle of the south side, and almost at the same instant seven mutineers — Job Anderson, the boatswain, at their head — broke into view, in full cry, at the southwestern corner.

They pulled up as if taken aback, and before they recovered, the squire and I, and Hunter and Joyce from the blockhouse, all had time to fire. The four shots went off in a rather ragged volley, but they did the work: one of the enemy dropped, and the rest, without a pause, turned and dived back into the trees.
Having reloaded, we walked down the outside of the palisade to see to the fallen man. He was stone dead — shot clean through the heart.

We were beginning to rejoice at our luck when, in that very moment, a pistol cracked in the bushes, a ball sang close past my ear, and poor Tom Redruth staggered and fell his full length on the ground. The squire and I both fired back, but having nothing to aim at, we likely only wasted powder. Then we reloaded and turned to poor Tom.
The captain and Gray were already over him, and I saw at half a glance that it was all up with him.

I believe the quickness of our return volley had scattered the mutineers once more, for we were let alone to lift the poor old gamekeeper over the stockade and carry him, groaning and bleeding, into the loghouse.

Poor old fellow — from the very first of our troubles down to this hour, when we laid him in the loghouse to die, he had never let fall one word of surprise, complaint, fear, or even of consent. He had lain like a Trojan behind his mattress in the gallery; he had obeyed every order silently, doggedly, and well; he was the oldest of our party by a score of years; and now it was he, the dour, old, faithful servant, who was to die.
The squire dropped on his knees beside him and kissed his hand, crying like a child.
“Am I going, doctor?” he asked.
“Tom, my man,” said I, “you're going home.”
“I wish I'd had a crack at them with the gun first,” he answered.
“Tom,” said the squire, “say you forgive me — won't you?”
“Would that be respectful-like, sir, from me to you?” came the answer. “But so be it — amen!”
After a short silence he said he thought somebody might read a prayer. “It's the custom, sir,” he added, as if apologizing. And not long after, without another word, he was gone.

Meanwhile the captain — whom I'd noticed to be wonderfully bulged about the chest and pockets — turned out a whole heap of odds and ends: the British colours, a Bible, a coil of stout rope, pen, ink, the log-book, and pounds of tobacco. He'd found a longish fir, felled and trimmed, lying in the enclosure, and with Hunter's help had set it up at the corner of the loghouse where the trunks crossed to make an angle. Then, climbing to the roof, he had with his own hands bent on and run up the colours.

This seemed a great relief to him. He came back into the loghouse and fell to counting up the stores, as if nothing else existed. But he kept an eye on Tom's passing all the same; and the moment it was over, he came forward with a second flag and reverently spread it over the body.
“Don't take on, sir,” he said, gripping the squire's hand. “All's well with him; no fear for a man shot down at his duty to captain and owner. It mayn't be sound divinity, but it's a fact.”
Then he drew me aside.
“Dr. Livesey,” said he, “in how many weeks do you and the squire look for the consort?”

I told him it was a matter not of weeks but of months: that if we weren't back by the end of August, Blandly was to send out to find us — but not before, and not after. “You can reckon it for yourself,” I said.
“Why, yes,” said the captain, scratching his head; “and making every allowance, sir, for the bounty of Providence, I'd call us pretty close-hauled.”
“How do you mean?” I asked.

“It's a pity, sir, we lost that second load — that's my meaning,” replied the captain. “For powder and shot, we'll do well enough. But the rations are short — very short; so short, Dr. Livesey, that we're maybe as well without that extra mouth.”
And he pointed to the dead body under the flag.
Just then, with a roar and a whistle, a round-shot flew high over the loghouse roof and came down far beyond us in the wood.
“Oho!” said the captain. “Blaze away! You've little enough powder as it is, my lads.”
At the next try the aim was truer, and the ball came down inside the stockade, throwing up a cloud of sand but doing no other harm.
“Captain,” said the squire, “the house is quite hidden from the ship. It must be the flag they're aiming at. Wouldn't it be wiser to haul it in?”

“Strike my colours?” cried the captain. “No, sir, not I.” And the moment he'd said it, I think we all agreed with him. For it wasn't only a piece of stout, seamanly good feeling; it was good policy too, and showed our enemies we cared nothing for their cannonade.

All through the evening they kept thundering away. Ball after ball flew over, or fell short, or kicked up the sand inside the enclosure; but they had to fire so high that the shot dropped spent and buried itself in the soft sand. We'd no ricochet to fear; and though one ball came in through the loghouse roof and out again through the floor, we soon grew used to that kind of rough play and minded it no more than a game of cricket.

“There's one good thing in all this,” said the captain. “The wood in front of us is likely clear. The ebb's been making a good while now; our stores should be uncovered. Volunteers to go and fetch in pork?”

Gray and Hunter were first to step forward. Well armed, they slipped out of the stockade — but the errand came to nothing. The mutineers were bolder than we'd reckoned, or trusted more to Israel's gunnery; for four or five of them were busy carrying off our stores and wading out with them to one of the gigs that lay close by, a man pulling an oar now and then to hold her against the current. Silver was in the stern-sheets, in command; and every one of them was now armed with a musket out of some secret store of their own.
The captain sat down to his log, and here is how the entry begins:

Alexander Smollett, master; David Livesey, ship's doctor; Abraham Gray, carpenter's mate; John Trelawney, owner; John Hunter and Richard Joyce, owner's servants and landsmen — being all that is left faithful of the ship's company — came ashore this day with stores for ten days at short rations, and flew the British colours over the loghouse on Treasure Island. Thomas Redruth, owner's servant and landsman, shot by the mutineers; James Hawkins, cabin-boy—
And at that very moment I was wondering what had become of poor Jim Hawkins.
A hail from the land side.
“Somebody hailing us,” said Hunter, who was on guard.
“Doctor! Squire! Captain! Hullo, Hunter — is that you?” came the cries.
And I reached the door just in time to see Jim Hawkins — safe and sound — come scrambling over the stockade.
